questions.q: What's different about this pipeline's use of an Eventstream compared to the dashboard pattern taught earlier in Fabric?
options: Eventstreams cannot be used for fraud detection
The consumer computes features from the stream as it flows, instead of landing raw events into an Eventhouse for a dashboard
The transaction data must first be converted to batch files
This pipeline doesn't use an Eventstream at all
questions.explain: The ingestion mechanism is the same Eventstream — what changes is that the consumer computes rolling features directly, to meet the scoring latency budget.

questions.q: Why does a tumbling window undercount a burst of transactions that straddles a window boundary?
options: Tumbling windows can only process one transaction at a time
Tumbling windows always overcount, never undercount
A tumbling window resets to zero at fixed boundaries, so the burst gets split across two windows instead of counted together
Tumbling windows require manual triggering
questions.explain: A sliding window avoids this because it recomputes continuously, so "the last 2 minutes" always reflects the actual most recent interval.

questions.q: What does the scoring model in the next lesson actually receive as input?
options: A nightly batch export of all transactions
The full raw transaction stream, unfiltered
Only the card ID, with no other data
Computed feature records (rolling counts and sums per card) — never raw transactions directly
questions.explain: Each new feature record produced by the sliding-window aggregation is what gets handed to scoring.

questions.q: What trade-off does setting a watermark's wait time actually control?
options: How long to wait for late-arriving events before finalizing a window — accuracy vs. staying inside the latency budget
How many card IDs can be processed simultaneously
The total retention period for raw events
Whether the Eventstream uses KQL or SQL
questions.explain: Too short a wait silently excludes real late transactions from a feature; too long a wait causes the feature to miss the scoring latency budget.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the watermark trade-off has no universally correct answer?
options: Because watermarks are optional and can always be skipped
Because the answer is always to wait as long as possible
Because late events never actually occur in production
Because it's a deliberate choice that depends on the specific latency budget and acceptable accuracy loss for this project
questions.explain: The right watermark setting depends on balancing accuracy against the sub-second budget set at kickoff — a choice that has to be made and documented, not derived from a formula.
